newsitem.title: IRAN: Iran needs better global ties to revive economy.
newsitem.headline: Iran needs better global ties to revive economy.

text.p: Iran has to improve ties with the West to attract the foreign capital essential for the economic revival President Mohammad Khatami is seeking, analysts said on Tuesday.
But they predicted tough resistance by hardliners to speedy moves to open up to the West and bring in much-needed foreign investment to tackle unemployment and inflation.
"We are obliged to open the door and have foreign capital come in," said businessman Amir Amini, a senior adviser at the Iran Chamber of Commerce, Industries and Mines.
"We, the state and the private sector, do not have the money to invest and create jobs," said Amini.
Inflation and unemployment are estimated by economists at double the official figures of 23 and 10 percent respectively.

Even if Khatami succeeded in resolving Iran's problems with western Europe sufficiently to attract capital, he would still face resistance from conservatives in parliament to any relaxation of the rules restricting foreign investment.

Khatami "has to do what he said he would do for the economy to start improving, but it is very difficult...more on the internal front" than in persuading Western powers to cooperate with Tehran, Amini said.

He was referring to Khatami's inaugural speech on Monday in which he sent conciliatory signals to the West, expressing a desire to cooperate with the rest of the world on the basis of mutual respect for traditions, religion and political system.
Khatami, 54, who took the oath of office on Monday, is a middle-level Shi'ite Moslem clergyman who is seen as a moderate among the ruling clergy.
Constitutionally he has until August 18 to present his cabinet to parliament for approval, a step which previous presidents have taken shortly after the oath.

"He is facing trouble from conservatives mainly over two ministers and I think this is delaying the announcement," an analyst said. Khatami started cabinet consultations immediately after his May election victory but has not yet announced his cabinet choices.

Conservative dailies have launched attacks against United Nations envoy Kamal Kharrazi, who told Reuters on Monday he had been aproached to head the foreign ministry, and Ataollah Mohajerani who is a candidate for the culture ministry.
Mohajerani came under severe attack in the late 1980s for proposing direct talks with the United States.

The evening hardline daily Kayhan on Tuesday attributed the delay to Khatami's determination to present parliament with a full cabinet list, dropping an earlier option of naming some acting ministers until a final decision is made.
Iran's Guardian Council, which vets all parliament decisions for conformity with Islam and the constitution, on Tuesday said the outgoing cabinet would continue as a caretaker government.

According to Iranian sources and local newspapers, current energy minister Bijan Namdar Zanganeh would replace Oil Minister Gholamreza Aghazadeh, in power since late 1985, and Hossein Namazi would be named finance and economy minister -- a post he held from 1982 to 1986.
"We have been circulating the same people since the (1979 Islamic) revolution. We need a fresh start, new faces all around," said one businessman who advocated drastic changes.
